articles.title: Photojournalist Steve Winter on his iconic Hollywood puma image, the illegal tiger trade and having a black panther knock on his door
articles.author: Hannah Osborne

paras.en: For decades, photojournalist Steve Winter has traveled across the world capturing incredible images of big cats as part of his work for National Geographic. Yet he didn't photograph an animal professionally until he was 34.

"If anybody had said, 'You're going to work with big cats for 25 years of your career,' I would have said 'No, I don't know anything about big cats,'" he told Live Science. "But I learned from scientists and local people," he added. "That was very, very important — that's what, to me, was the biggest change in my life."

Together with his wife, author and environmental journalist Sharon Guynup, Winter has helped change laws around big cats in the U.S.; revealed the horrors of the Tiger Temple in Bangkok, resulting in its closure; and took an iconic photograph of the cougar P-22 beneath the Hollywood sign, which eventually led to the creation of the world's largest highway wildlife corridor over Highway 101 in California.

In their new book, "Big Cats" (National Geographic Books, 2026), Winter and Guynup provide a retrospective of their careers, looking at the fragility of these predators, the conservation work helping to save them, and the challenges they still face. Live Science spoke with Winter about his career, the changes he's seen, and why he's hopeful for the future.
Hannah Osborne: You've traveled all over the world and seen so many things. Is there one photograph that really sticks out for you, one that you come back to and think about?

Steve Winter: I always look at the images that have had an impact at the time. That makes a huge difference to me, because in the end, I know that in taking this [photograph], not only did I succeed beyond my wildest expectations, but it's making a difference in the world. Right now, I have just been putting remote cameras up on what will be the world's largest wildlife overpass, and that was started by my Hollywood cougar picture of P-22, Puma 22, under the Hollywood sign. [Editor's note: The common names cougar, puma and mountain lion all refer to the same species, Puma concolor.]
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That changed so much in Los Angeles. I've never seen a city be transformed in their love for the fact that they have a mountain lion in a park in the city. What came of that was [people] thinking, "Hey, maybe we should connect these areas where these animals are living." [Editor's note: The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing over the 10-lane Highway 101 that was inspired by the cougar P-22 is due to open Dec. 2.]
To think about that is pretty amazing, so right now, P-22 and the Hollywood cougar is my go-to image.

He became a celebrity in the land of celebrities; people loved him. There's a P-22 day; schools are using urban wildlife in their curriculum. The LA Natural History Museum has a permanent exhibit, and what is right in the center of it? The Hollywood cougar picture.
HO: How did the P-22 photograph come about?

SW: As wildlife photographers, we will often go to these meetings where people are gathering to save elephants, to save this, to save that. So I went to meet the scientists that worked with these cats in the largest urban park in the United States. I asked Jeff Sikich, a biologist for the National Park Service, "[Do] you have a lot of trails in that park? Do you have any that the cats walk on where you could see the lights of LA in the background?" He kept saying no.

When you're working with camera traps, it's very important to visualize the picture in your mind that you're after [when] you visit a spot. I just said, "Well, Jeff, you know what would really tell the story of urban wildlife is if we had a mountain lion under the Hollywood sign." He looked at me like I'm crazy, and said, "There's no mountain lions in Griffith Park." I said, "If anything changes, let me know."
Eight months later, I got a text. They had a trail camp set up to census bobcats [Lynx rufus] in the park, and there was P-22.

With camera traps, you don't need to sit, and I learned that from the beginning. For the second story I did, it was photographing a quetzal, which is a sacred bird of the Maya and the Aztecs. I knew nothing about birds, either. It's got a meter-long [3 feet] tail. I was enamored by the fact that it had a historical background — they used quetzal feathers as a form of currency; they were sacred birds.

I loved all that, but working on that story in a cloud forest in Guatemala on top of a mountain all by myself, every morning I'd come down and set my camera up on the tripod [near the bird's nest], and then take it away at the end of the day. I'd walk back, and all of a sudden, the hair on the back of my head would stand up and on my arm, and I'd get this tingling feeling and it's like, what's going on? I'd turn around. You can't see anything in a rainforest or a cloud forest because the proliferation of life is everywhere. One night when I'm reading my book in the one room shack that I was staying in my bunk bed, all I hear is the stairs creaking. Then I hear the floorboards creaking. Then I hear scratching, and then sniffing, outside the door.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: I grabbed the walkie-talkie to call Juan Carlos, the naturalist that I was working with. He would find the quetzal nests for me. I asked him, in Spanish, "Juan Carlos, what is this?"

And he said, "Oh, Steve, don't worry; it's just a black panther [Panthera onca]." I've been there five weeks, and I said, "Well, how come it took you so long to tell me there was a black jaguar here?" And he said, "We didn't want to worry you."

HO: Throughout the book, you look at topics like poaching, captive tigers in the Tiger Temple in Thailand, and the way they're kept in the U.S. for entertainment. And a lot of these things are still going on. How do you cope with seeing that side of their lives?

SW: When I was first working on tigers, I was in Thailand. I was wanting to work in Thailand and Sumatra because they were the two subspecies that experts said may go extinct. I was working with the most incredible group of scientists I've probably ever worked with. They were trying to save the Indo-Chinese tiger [Panthera tigris corbetti] in Thailand.

But close by was this place called the Thai Tiger Temple. And I said, "Hey, guys; I'd like to go there." And they said, "No, Steve; don't go. These are bad people, and we think they're involved in the black-market trade of tiger parts and tigers to Laos and then into China."

That's a good reason for me to go if you don't want me to go. The first thing I saw was this huge sign that said "conservation." This was a Buddhist monastery. For some reason, the abbot had been given a tiger cub about 10 years before, and he fell in love with tigers. So they started a tiger tourism operation that brought in at least $3 million a year.

I could see something was fishy right away, because by then, I'd learned a lot about these cats. They kept saying that they always had 150 tigers. But you could pet tiger cubs for Instagram selfies or bottle-feed them 365 days a year. If you're breeding tigers, what are you going to have? More tigers. Something was happening to them, because the death rate wouldn't take over the birth rate when you're speed-breeding cubs, which is what they were doing. A female has cubs; they take them away immediately so she'll be ready to have another litter. You can only use the cubs for three months because after that, they're too big to pet.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: They had all these tourist things where you could get a selfie with a head of a tiger in your lap. I was saying, "Why are these tigers acting so sleepy?" They're taking this giant head of a tiger and putting it in somebody's lap that's sitting on the concrete. You would think that if you put the head of a tiger in your lap, you're going to end up with your head in their mouth.

[Editor's note: Winter and Guynup worked together on an investigation into the Tiger Temple in 2016, which eventually led to it being exposed for its abuse and connections with the illegal wildlife trade. Shortly after, the Tiger Temple was shut to the public.]

Sharon did the investigation, and I already had pictures. But we went to do a video and go visit the temple again … By the time we got done, the TV stations in Bangkok had taken the video and showed it all over on the nightly news. We kept working on this, and Sharon wrote four more stories. And after the last one, the Thai government was inundated with people calling for the prime minister to shut it down. They went in with the army and the police, and what they found was horrific. They went to the freezer. There were tigers hanging on meat hooks, cubs in jars, with a little Thai flag on them. They shut it down.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Stopping this is really important. After that, we did a story on tigers in the U.S., which was very difficult psychologically. It was one thing to see them in Thailand, but we had always heard that there were more tigers in the United States than there are in the wild, and people would go, "What are you talking about? We don't have tigers here."

Sharon and I … we found a lot of the same speed-breeding cubs at these roadside zoos, whether it was Doc Antle's Myrtle Beach that was $500 a day, or some dumpy little place on the road down south where you can give them $10 to look at a tiger. They were everywhere.

After that story came out, the National Geographic Society gave a copy of this 30-page story that we had done for the magazine to every member of Congress. We got this text on 20th December, 2022, that President Biden had signed the Big Cat Public Safety Act, which outlawed all that. We were part of getting this law passed, which was incredible.
HO: What are some of the biggest changes in conservation you've seen over your career?

SW: Conservation was changing a lot in the '90s and 2000s. Alan Rabinowitz [a zoologist who served as the president, CEO and chief scientist at Panthera Corp., a nonprofit conservation organization devoted to protecting wild cats] had this idea after he had a lot of scientists in Central and South America give him data on where they were working and where jaguars were. When he took it away and just showed the locations, he goes, this is a corridor, a natural corridor, because now we're talking a lot about connectivity and how roads get in the way. It's like animals are in prison because they can't cross these big freeways or even small ones. Find out where animals are, their migrating paths, and put in an overpass or an underpass or something.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: All this was happening, all this new science, new conservation. That was all spearheaded by the work of [biologist and conservationist] George Schaller, who became a friend of ours. What a life that we've had — and are having. We're still working on the connectivity part right now.
HO: Are you hopeful for the big cats in LA?

SW: Oh, definitely. The ones that live in the Santa Monica National Recreation Area will be able to cross the 101 and then go all the way to San Jose. They could actually then hug the top of a certain mountain and get close to San Francisco, which is incredible to think about now. It's a huge metropolitan area, so you're leaving one, going to another. But there's so much land in between, and they can cross safely.

- 'If you do want to be a criminal, there is no better place to do it': Author Rose George dives into the dark depths of the fishing industry
- 'If this is the new normal, then we are in very deep trouble': Brazil's drying aquifers could have ripple effects across the world
HO: What made you specialize in big cats in the first place, and what's the draw that keeps you coming back?

SW: Big cats are so charismatic and, to me, mystical. And they're an umbrella species, so if you save the largest predator, which is usually a big cat in any landscape, you save everything underneath it.

I was just taken over by these animals. National Geographic had never done a jaguar story before. I found out really quick why: You can't see them. I tried to use remote cameras, camera traps, but they're really smart. They'll go around them, so they don't have the flash going off or they don't like the sound or the smell of meat on these waterproof boxes and the cords and all that.

I just fell in love with big cats, and what a life to be able to work with every one of them. The only one that was on my list that I haven't done is the Amur tiger, Siberian tiger [Panthera tigris altaica]. When I was ready to photograph them with the scientists that had been monitoring them for over a decade, [the tigers] got canine distemper and about 60% died.

Big cats really bounce back when you give them protection, and there was protection given after you lose this many. All the study tigers that had the GPS collars on, the ones they could monitor, died. But the population bounced back, and there's more now than there were before.

I won't get to photograph Amur tigers. And the reason is, there's people — locals — who are working on it, and they're doing an incredible job. I've got a book here that has all the cats that I've worked on. The impact these stories have had, and the change that's come about, is what really makes me proud.
This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

National Geographic photographer Steve Winter has spent his career photographing big cats around the world, from the graceful jaguars of Brazil’s Pantanal to the elusive Himalayan snow leopard. His photographs astound; his stories, even more so. In Big Cats, Winter and environmental journalist Sharon Guynup share experiences behind the lens.

In chapters on every key species—cougar, jaguar, leopard, snow leopard, tiger, and lion—readers will witness the power of Winter’s work, including uplifting stories of how his photographs have made a difference and powered important conservation efforts on behalf of these mighty creatures.

Hannah Osborne is the planet Earth and animals editor at Live Science. Prior to Live Science, she worked for several years at Newsweek as the science editor. Before this she was science editor at International Business Times U.K. Hannah holds a master's in journalism from Goldsmith's, University of London.

articles.title: These South American Birds Can Match a Jackhammer's Ear-Splitting Volume, Making Them Some of the World's Loudest Known Avians

paras.en: From soft peeps to piercing calls, birds produce a wide range of sounds. But scientists recently discovered that two South American species take their calls to ear-splitting extremes, making deafening vocalizations on par with a jackhammer.

The bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema can produce sounds at amplitudes that exceed 120 decibels, according to a study published September 29 in the journal Evolution. They’re now among the ranks of the white bellbird, another South American species, for the loudest known birds on the planet.

Researchers behind the new work didn’t specifically set out to find the world’s noisiest birds. Rather, they wanted to take advantage of recent technological advancements that have made it easier to measure vocal amplitude, the height of a sound wave and a key element of loudness.

“Until recently, it was very impractical to go out into the field and measure amplitude,” lead author João Menezes, an evolutionary biologist who conducted the research while at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, tells the New York Times’ Taylor Mitchell Brown. “It’s kind of stepping into a whole new world.”

The researchers started the project in Amherst, Massachusetts, during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when the unusually quiet circumstances made it easier to isolate and record bird song. They used a laser rangefinder to measure their distance from a specific bird, as well as a sound level meter, which allowed them to isolate that bird’s call from other noises.

“Even recording from my window or from the backyard, almost always that would be [the amplitude of] a new species,” Menezes tells the Washington Post’s Meghan Bartels. “It’s not often that you get to do this kind of exploratory science where you just go out into the field and document things for the first time, especially with birds.”

From Massachusetts, they headed next to Brazil, where they recorded birds in several different habitats. The scientists ultimately collected amplitude data on 123 bird species between December 2018 and January 2025, filling a major gap in scientists’ understanding of how loud birds can sing. Previously, scientists only had amplitude data for ten of those species—even the ubiquitous Canada goose had never been measured.

“We’ve been able to vastly increase the number of species for which there is amplitude data,” study co-author Jeffrey Podos, also an evolutionary biologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, says in a statement. “This is basic, foundational research that no one else has managed to do on this scale.”

Their amplitude database captures the impressive range of bird vocalization volumes. At the low end, they documented the dusky-throated hermit, a hummingbird that buzzes at a modest 64 decibels, about the same volume as a normal conversation. At the high end, the bare-throated bellbird and red-legged seriema are both about as loud as a trumpeting elephant or a chainsaw.

Comparing the amplitude data with the birds’ anatomy revealed that species with bigger bodies and wider mouth openings also tended to be the loudest. This is probably because “bigger birds have bulkier muscles, which are capable of creating greater internal pressures, which ultimately generate louder sounds, and then broader mouths allow more energy to radiate into the environment,” Menezes tells CNN’s Amarachi Orie.

Still, the researchers have many unanswered questions. The big one: Why are some birds so much louder than others? The researchers hypothesized that the loudest birds evolved their high-volume calls to attract numerous mates, or to communicate through dense vegetation. But those explanations don’t hold up for the red-legged seriema, so there must be some other factor driving the evolution of its loud vocalizations.

“The seriema is the opposite of those two things,” Menezes tells WBUR’s Barbara Moran. “It’s a super open-habitat bird, like pasture, and it’s strictly monogamous. So, it forms a pair for the breeding season, and that’s it.”

There’s no single answer to the question of which species holds the title of “world’s loudest bird”—it depends on how researchers define loudness. The bare-throated bellbird, for example, produced the loudest individual call, reaching nearly 131 decibels, per CNN. But when researchers averaged the loudest calls across individual birds, the red-legged seriema came out on top at nearly 121 decibels. Averaging the vocalizations’ peak volumes, on the other hand, allowed the white bellbird to take the lead at 127 decibels.

paras.en: Scientists are still unraveling the evolutionary underpinnings of super loud birdsong. But in the meantime, their work could have important implications for conservation. For example, reliable amplitude data could help researchers use audio recordings to determine not just whether a species is present, but also how close those birds might be and how many individuals are nearby, Connor Wood, an ornithologist at Cornell University who wasn’t involved in the study, tells the Washington Post.
The findings could also help scientists better understand how birds may adapt to a changing world.

“Amplitude is so critical to the ability of birds to communicate with each other, that it is really important for us to understand exactly how that might be able to change,” Nathan Senner, an ornithologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst who also wasn’t involved with the study, tells WBUR. “How they evolve is really fundamental to our understanding of how they might continue to evolve as our world changes.”

articles.title: A Community-Led Archaeology Dig on a Tiny Scottish Isle Has Unearthed a Medieval Monastery of 'International Importance'

paras.en: Historians have long known that Lismore, a small isle in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland, was home to a medieval monastery called Lios Mòr. Written records detail its sixth-century founding by St. Mo Luóc, one of the early monks who spread Christianity to northern Britain. But with very little archaeological evidence, apart from a broken granite cross, scholars could not confirm Lios Mòr’s size, style or significance—until now.

According to an article published in the journal Antiquity last week, a group of local volunteers led by archaeologist Clare Ellis, of the firm Argyll Archaeology, discovered an early medieval cemetery, various structures and “sophisticated craftworking of international importance” during excavations near Lismore’s 13th-century parish church.

“For centuries, Lismore’s early monastery was known mainly from written records and local tradition,” study co-author Gordon Noble, an archaeologist at the University of Aberdeen, says in a statement. “We can now see that it was a thriving center of worship, craftsmanship and learning, whose importance may have rivaled some of the best-known monasteries in early medieval Britain.”

Lismore’s historical society began searching for the site of Mo Luóc’s monastery in 2016. A “dynamic minority” of the island’s 170 or so residents crowdfunded and ran the digs, Robert Hay, a retired local scientist and dig participant, tells the Guardian’s Esther Addley. Grants, donations and yet more crowdfunding enabled the enthusiastic locals to hire Ellis to lead excavations near the site of Lismore’s 13th-century church, which still holds services.

“The research aimed to determine whether the site of the later medieval cathedral at Lismore was also the location of Mo Luóc’s early monastery, and to assess the scale, nature and status of the settlement,” Ellis says in the statement.

The dig uncovered a medieval cemetery containing at least six burials radiocarbon dated to between 650 and 1040 C.E. The archaeologists also unearthed a piece of an “early medieval cross slab,” per the study. In another area, they found more human remains and additional fragments of carved stone crosses.

“This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment,” Noble tells the Guardian. He compares it to Scotland’s famed Iona monastery, which was founded in 563 C.E. Both settlements were products of a medieval missionary movement that aimed to spread Christianity throughout pagan Britain. The monks succeeded. By the seventh century, Britain was Christianized.

Elsewhere on the cathedral property, researchers found the remains of an oval-shaped building paved with a layer of limestone. Dated to between the seventh and tenth centuries, it contained remnants of craftwork, handmade pottery, struck flint and an antler.

Another trench boasted extensive evidence of precious metalwork: more than 1,000 pieces of debris, including well-preserved molds and crucibles once used to melt down and cast gold, copper and silver. Hay describes them as “the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland,” per the Guardian.

Clay molds and crucibles are “unusual” finds for a monastic site, Noble tells Scientific American’s Jackie Flynn Mogensen. “It’s one of the largest metalworking assemblages we have from any site, secular or sacred, in this time period,” he adds.

The Lismore monastery appears to have an unusually large footprint. This, coupled with evidence of precious metals and craftsmanship, suggests the community was actually considerably wealthy and “far more than a small island church,” per the statement.
As Noble says to Scientific American, Lios Mòr appears to have been “a very significant mover and shaker” in its day. “It’ll be really exciting to see what shows up in the coming years.”

articles.title: September's Ozone Hole Was the Biggest It Has Been in 25 Years

paras.en: In September, the Antarctic ozone hole peaked at 10.6 million square miles—the second largest ever observed for this time of year.

Using data from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, scientists found that the ozone hole started growing earlier than usual in August. By September 20, it reached a size close to its October 2015 peak, when it was 10.8 million square miles.

To understand what’s happening, we first need to understand the ozone layer. The ozone layer lies in the Earth’s stratosphere and protects our planet from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation that can harm humans, plants and animals. The infamous ozone hole is actually a patch of depleted ozone in the stratosphere over Antarctica that is mainly caused by chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs. While the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out the use of CFCs globally, they can persist in the atmosphere for decades.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The ozone hole’s size fluctuates every year. For about three months each fall—the Southern Hemisphere’s spring—the hole opens inside the stratospheric polar vortex, a large band of fast-spinning westerly winds that encircles Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. The vortex traps freezing air inside and leads to the formation of polar stratospheric clouds, writes a New Zealand-based research team in The Conversation. “Chemical reactions on particles in this rare type of cloud then activate ozone-depleting gases,” they add.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This year brought a stronger and colder polar vortex. “We have unusually strong winds and cold temperatures over the pole that have created the conditions possible for the hole to grow to the size it has today,” research team member Hannah Kessenich, a physicist at the University of Otago in New Zealand, tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC News). By late January, the hole will shrink again.
Did you know? Wildfires can destroy the ozone layer

- Climate change has increased the frequency of wildfires, which is not a good thing when it comes to mending the ozone layer. A study published in Nature in 2023 found that particles in wildfire smoke spark chemical reactions in the atmosphere that break down ozone.

So, should we be worried? “This year’s ozone hole shouldn’t be a cause for alarm,” Kessenich told Live Science's Sascha Pare in an email. “However, there are still many unanswered questions. It’s something we need to keep a close eye on.”

Kessenich and other experts underscore the fact that the ozone hole size we’re currently seeing isn’t a sign that the Montreal Protocol isn’t working. “We look at the depth of the hole rather than the area to assess how we’re coming along in terms of the recovery from those chemicals,” Kessenich says to ABC News.

In fact, this year’s hole isn’t as deep as it has been in previous years, and year-to-year variability is to be expected. “We have to look at the longer term trends, and those metrics continue to tell us that the ozone hole is slowly recovering as expected,” adds Susan Solomon, an atmospheric chemist at MIT, in an email to Live Science.

There will, however, be impacts on weather across the Southern Hemisphere. A larger ozone hole shifts the Southern Annular Mode into a positive phase, which affects winds and precipitation in different areas. In Australia, for example, it causes increased rainfall on the country’s southeast coast, Kessenich and her colleagues write in The Conversation.

Researchers are still trying to understand how climate change impacts the strength of the polar vortex, and why bigger ozone holes are persisting longer than they used to. It could be that changes in global atmospheric dynamics are making longer-lived ozone holes more likely, which in turn could mean our timelines for ozone recovery need to be adapted.
“It's too soon to tell what has been driving dynamical variability in recent years, but more research is needed,” Kessenich says to Live Science.

articles.title: The Best Smart Scales for Tracking Weight and Body Composition (2026)
articles.author: Christopher Null

paras.en: After years of sleepiness, the smart scale world has finally woken up—driven almost certainly by the GLP-1 craze, as millions of consumers find themselves wondering if those weekly jabs are actually working.

What was previously a category occupied by dated gear has abruptly exploded, and for good reason. Today’s smart scales don’t just report on your weight; they do things like measure your heart rate and break down muscle composition, and some can even give you an eye on your heart health, courtesy of technology like integrated ECG systems. Through mobile apps, they can track all of this information over time.

The big shift in the category in the past year has been a flood of new full-body scanners hitting the market from all corners. Essentially bathroom scales with handlebar-based scanners, these don’t just use bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) to measure conductivity (and, thus, body fat percentage) through your feet. They can now scan through your hands, too, giving you a much more holistic (and ostensibly accurate) look at your body metrics than a floor scale will provide. I’ve personally seen body fat percentage numbers swing up to 6 percent between the two types of scales. (Spoiler: The full-body scanner data is always higher.)
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Do you really need all that information? I’ve long suggested that it’s really the trend line that matters most, not the absolute numbers, and as long as your metrics are headed in the right direction, it doesn’t matter quite as much whether things are off by a small percentage. Consistent weigh-ins are the most important part of the process, along with tracking that information over time to determine whether your diet and workout regimen (or medication routine) is getting you the results you need.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Mind you, scale prices are headed up, and new full-body scanners can now top $600 for top-tier tech. That’s part of the reason why I still recommend a standard scale for most users, as these devices are considerably less expensive, and the results they offer are likely to be good enough for all but serious athletes.
Either way, this roundup has an option for every type of user.
Updated October 2026: I've added Withings’ BodyScan 2 and new honorable mentions from Runstar, Tanita, and Withings. I've also added scales to avoid and ensured up-to-date prices throughout.

Smart scales come in two basic flavors: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. The former connects directly to your phone to sync its readings. The latter uses your home’s wireless network to sync readings straight to the cloud, which your phone’s app can then access. Wi-Fi scales are generally more expensive but more versatile. While older scales often featured erratic wireless connections, newer models have many of their kinks worked out—and firmware updates have improved connectivity.

Virtually all smart scales use the same type of system to gauge your additional vitals: bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), which involves sending a minuscule electric current up one leg and measuring what happens when it comes down the other side. Some mathematical magic converts all of this into any number of derived measurements about things like your body’s percentage of fat, water, and bone; body-mass index (BMI); and, sometimes, arcana like your basal metabolic rate (BMR), which is a measure of your body’s energy consumption at rest. All the scales I tested can sync data with Apple Health and Google's Health Connect, either directly or by passing data via the app.

paras.en: When Is the Best Time to Weigh Yourself?

Most experts say that the best time to weigh in is first thing in the morning, before you’ve eaten and after you’ve used the restroom. The main reason for this is consistency: Weighing yourself at the same time every day is the best way to ensure that consecutive weigh-ins are taken under conditions that are as controlled as possible. Since eating and drinking will cause your weight to fluctuate considerably, weighing yourself on an empty stomach means you’re getting an apples-to-apples comparison each morning.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: As a small bonus, your weight is usually at its lowest right after you wake up, so you potentially stand to give yourself a gentle confidence boost by stepping on the scale then instead of after dinner.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Renpho MorphoScan for $170: The Renpho MorphoScan full-body scanner looks surprisingly similar to the Runstar FG2015, including a near-identical display attached to the handlebars. Well, spoiler alert: They are basically the same scale. They even use the same app to collect data (you can use both scales simultaneously with the app).

Runstar Smart Body Fat Scale (FG2015) for $140: My former pick for best full-body scanner, this admittedly garish offering tracks 20 metrics and supports 24 users, effectively breaking down information, limb-by-limb, in its Starfit mobile app. USB-C rechargeability is a nice plus, but the price tag—just $140 if you buy it directly from Runstar—is probably its best feature.

Tanita RD-953 InnerScan Pro for $230: One of the few new feet-only smart scales to hit the market this decade, Tanita’s RD-953 is defined by its Cylonesque looks—and its relative simplicity. The costly Bluetooth-only scale scans quickly, though the placement of its display in the center of the scale, right between your feet, can be awkward for those with even a small breadbasket between their head and the floor. I also didn’t love the very high and hopefully overstated body fat reading the scale gave me, but my harshest criticism is directed at the Healthy Edge app (a different app than is used by Tanita’s other scale), which is about as engaging and motivational as a shopping list on a Post-It Note.

paras.en: Withings BodyFit for $230: The middle child in the Withings family sits comfortably between the no-holds-barred BodyScan 2 and the feet-only Body Comp Smart Scale, offering a pleasant alternative for users who want full-body analysis but don’t need (or want to pay for) the fitness extremism of Withings’s top-tier model. It’s a sleek and demure unit with a small but informative color screen, quick Wi-Fi connectivity, and fast performance—and, of course, it works seamlessly with Withings’s excellent app.

paras.en: Arboleaf Body Fat Scale CS20W for $50: This affordable Bluetooth scale isn’t the most eye-catching I’ve tested in light of its big silver electrodes and an oversized display that comes across as a bit garish. While weight is easy to make out, the six additional statistics showcased are difficult to read, all displayed simultaneously. I like the Arboleaf app better than the scale, where five additional metrics are available, each featuring a helpful explanation when tapped. It’s a solid deal at this price, but the upsell to get an “intelligent interpretation report” for an extra $40 per year is probably safe to skip.

paras.en: Hume Health Body Pod for $229: Hume Health’s Body Pod, another full-body scanner with handles, is heavily advertised—at least to the apps on my phone—and touted (by Hume) as the Next Big Thing in the world of body management. While the app is indeed glossy and inviting, I was shocked to discover how flimsy the hardware felt, that it lacked Wi-Fi, and that some features are locked behind a $100-a-year Hume Plus subscription plan. It works fine enough, but you can get results that are just as good with a cheaper device.

paras.en: Garmin Index S2 for $200: Five years after its release, the Index S2 is still Garmin’s current model, a surprise for a company otherwise obsessed with fitness. It’s still noteworthy for its lovely color display, which walks you through its six body metrics (for up to 16 users) with each weigh-in. The display also provides your weight trend over time in graphical form and can even display the weather. The scale connects directly to Wi-Fi and Garmin’s cloud-based storage system, so—unlike with Bluetooth-only scales—you don’t need a phone nearby to track your progress. A phone running the Garmin Connect app (Android, iOS) is handy, so you can keep track of everything over time. Unfortunately, as health apps go, Connect is a bit of a bear, so expect a learning curve—especially if you want to make changes to the way the scale works. You can turn its various LCD-screen widgets on or off in the app, but finding everything can be difficult due to the daunting scope of the Garmin ecosystem. The color screen is nice at first, but it ultimately adds little to the package.

paras.en: Omron BCM-500 for $85: With its large LCD panel, quartet of onboard buttons, and oversize silver electrodes, the Omron BCM-500 is an eye-catching masterwork of brutalist design. If your bathroom is decked out in concrete and wrought iron, this scale will fit right in. The Bluetooth unit syncs with Omron’s HeartAdvisor app (Android, iOS), but it provides all six of its body metrics directly on the scale, cycling through them with each weigh-in (for up to four users). It can be difficult to read the label for each of the data points, in part because the LCD isn’t backlit, but the app is somewhat easier to follow, offering front-page graphs of weight, skeletal muscle, and body fat. On the other hand, the presentation is rather clinical, and the app is surprisingly slow to sync. For a scale without a Wi-Fi connection, it’s also rather expensive.

If this were a mega-bargain in line with foot-only scale pricing, I’d be sold, but the meager savings compared to other MorphoScan scales don’t justify considering it.

The Bluetooth-only scale is confusing to set up and difficult to use correctly, and I was only able to get successful measurements by first opening the mobile app and ensuring the scale was connected before carefully stepping onto it. Then, I had to wait for a prompt to pick up the handles (while balanced on the device). Testing feels like it takes forever, and that’s even if you get it right the first time. For $480, the scale is a questionable value at best, despite its 40 measurements offered. No Wi-Fi at this price, really?

articles.title: Best Lego Gifts for Brick Builders (2026): Smart Bricks, Video Games, and More
articles.author: Simon Hill

paras.en: Lego isn't going anywhere. Those beloved little bricks won't biodegrade, are machined to incredibly tight tolerances, and—unless your dog chews one up—retain what Lego refers to as their “clutch power” for decades. Their relevance in terms of cultural pastiche isn’t fading on me either. They're as irresistible to me today as they were as a kid.
If you and your loved ones are also obsessed with Lego sets, we have some great gift ideas. For more recommendations, don't forget to check out our other gift guides.
Updated October 2026: I added the Lego Ideas Peanuts: Snoopy's Doghouse, a Lego Batman game, Star Wars Advent Calendar 2026, Star Trek light kit, and Lego Architecture Paris: City of Love.

- Their Favorite Themed Set One of the reasons that Lego sets are so popular is the company's innumerable licensing deals. No matter what you're into, Lego has signed a deal to make a Lego set about it. (And then, in an ouroboros of advertising, the company will then make a movie about the Lego set about the franchise.) Anyway, this is a long and roundabout way of saying that my son and I are obsessed with the Lego Formula 1 sets. I even got to watch the Lego cars hit the track at a Formula 1 race. Ever since then, we've been watching the races and Netflix's Drive to Survive. It's the perfect collaboration because Lego bricks and Formula 1 engineers are on the same page when it comes to precise engineering and tight tolerances. Also, once you're done building, the cars work as toys as well as sets. —Adrienne So

articles.title: AI Is Getting Really Good at Messing With Cybercriminals
articles.author: Lily Hay Newman, Matt Burgess

paras.en: Even as AI supercharges digital scamming and cybercrime, it’s also being recruited in the fight to protect potential victims. Governments around the world have consistently struggled to address the global crisis of online crime, grappling with the limitations of attempting to crack down on criminals beyond their borders. This has inspired alternative efforts, like using automation to attempt to go after scammers en masse—perhaps by spamming the spammers to squander their resources. Now, AI platforms are turning these types of experiments into real tools in the fight against cybercrime.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: For the last two years, the Australian company Apate, named after the Greek goddess of deception, has been building a system that diverts phone scammers onto calls with AI bots that are trained to keep conversations going as long as possible without, of course, ever actually falling for the scam. The goal is to give scammers enough hope that they stay on the phone, while also collecting intelligence about the scams they’re running.

“What we really like to think is that we’re building the perfect victims for scammers,” Dali Kaafar, the founder and CEO of Apate, tells us. “A minute that a scammer is talking to a bot or an agent is a minute where you’re probably saving hundreds, if not thousands of possible people being reached out to by that exact same scammer,” he says, referencing the ability for scammers to use automated dialing tools.

Kaafar says Apate’s platform, which is used by banks and supported by telecom companies, has around 350,000 bots. They not only pick up calls, but also infiltrate scam chat groups online and respond to text messages with similar goals of frustrating scammers while collecting intelligence from them. He says the company has collected more than 250,000 pieces of information about fraudsters in real-time, from scam URLs to money mule accounts and bank details.

The bots have different personalities, language skills, and profiles, Kaafar says, so scammers hopefully don’t detect that they’re conversing with an AI. Like real people, “sometimes [the bots] do have WhatsApp, sometimes they don’t. Sometimes they pick up the phone, sometimes they just actually hang up on the scammer saying, ‘I'll come back to you later,’” he says.

But are they convincing? Kernel Panic tested the tool using a demo version where users play the role of the scammer and talk to one of Apate’s AI “victims.” The personas are designed to express a healthy amount of skepticism but leave enough openings for scammers to continue to try to win them over, a dynamic that we could immediately feel and found intensely frustrating.

Scammers are likely familiar with this type of skeptical interaction, and Kaafar says that Apate calls regularly go on for more than two hours. In our testing, the Apate system was engaged and responsive, and the timing of the conversation felt natural, even with both of us tag-teaming the AI as a friend, “Lucy,” and her financial adviser “Mickey.” We did not succeed at getting the Apate AI system to invest in our cryptocurrency opportunity even after six minutes of diligent effort. (The returns are truly incredible, though, we swear.)
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: For now, even with Apate’s massive swarm of bots on the case, it’s only a matter of time before you get your next scam call or text. Cybercriminals initiate billions of messages and calls each year, with the most sophisticated operations running physical, industrial scale scamming sites. And while professional scambaiters and initiatives to infiltrate scam operations have done critical deterrent work for years, law enforcement and research efforts haven’t been able to stop the expansion of digital scamming overall.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But AI could create a new era for anti-scam efforts, not just scammers themselves. Better intelligence sharing between cops, social media companies, banks, and other industries is desperately needed and could potentially be aided by AI-driven monitoring and data analysis. Increasingly, too, innovative efforts have been looking to disrupt cybercriminals by exploiting their “psychological vulnerabilities.” In some cases, these psyops have included directly trolling those behind ransomware attacks. As the focus on disrupting scammers and cybercriminals expands, the use of generative AI as a way to keep them preoccupied, wasting resources, and not launching other attacks appears to be increasingly effective.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Take honeypots, for instance. For years, companies and security researchers have deployed false virtual machines to attract hackers, waste their time, gather information, and understand their secret hacking techniques. Mark Vero, a doctoral researcher at the department of computer science at ETH Zurich, says open source honeypot providers have increasingly been incorporating LLMs into their systems to make them appear more realistic.

In recent research, Vero and colleagues found an LLM-powered honey pot would keep AI agents attacking their system “significantly longer” than a honey pot with more predictable behavior. “The agentic attackers are much more convinced by the LLM simulated honeypots and they also mark them as actual honeypots at a much lower rate,” he says. “If these systems are built well enough, then I think it’s quite advantageous for defenders.”
Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

articles.title: Reedus: Filming final scenes of 'Daryl Dixon' felt like an accomplishment

paras.en: NEW YORK, Oct. 10 (UPI) -- The Walking Dead legends Norman Reedus and Melissa McBride appeared at New York Comic Con Friday to talk about their 15-year journey as zombie-apocalypse survivors Daryl and Carol.
The stars played the best friends for 11 seasons of the flagship TWD series, which took place in the American southwest, and for four seasons of the European spin-off, Daryl Dixon.
Season 4 has already been filmed and premieres in February. The final season is being billed as "one last journey, one last fight."
"It was super-weird, the whole last week [of filming,]" Reedus, 57, told UPI at a New York Comic Con press conference Friday.

"Not to give spoilers away in any way, whatsoever. But it was sad. It was an accomplishment. It felt like that quote from David Bowie, when they say, 'What do you think your last words are going to be when you die?' And he goes, 'But, but, but...' It was a little bit like that," the actor recalled.

"But it felt like an accomplishment. It felt like we told the story we were trying to tell and it was sad for the crew, too. You become this really big family, especially when we're going overseas and hanging around new people in a new place and it was very emotional all the way."

"There were three things: there was Melissa's last scene and there was Norman's last scene and there's the last scene they did together," executive producer David Zabel said. "So, there's sort of three things, each of which was emotionally different."
McBride added, "And Norman's last scene was the last shot we ever shot as a show."
Zabel said that just because this chapter of The Walking Dead is over, doesn't mean there aren't still stories in this universe to tell.
"There will still be shows," executive producer Scott M. Gimple said. "See what's in them."

articles.title: Christa Pike released from hospital after 10 days

paras.en: Oct. 10 (UPI) -- Christa Pike, who survived a botched execution attempt, was released from the hospital Saturday, 10 days later.
She was transferred back to the prison in Nashville where she was held before her execution.

"Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years," her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement Saturday. "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery."
Pike, 50, was the first woman Tennessee tried to execute in more than 200 years on Sept. 30. She received two doses of pentobarbital, each of which could have been lethal.

Pike survived the injections and was seen by witnesses snoring and breathing. She was taken to the hospital in critical condition and unconscious. Her lawyers had believed she was brain dead, but she woke up and began speaking on Oct. 6. On Thursday, her lawyer said she was up and walking in the hospital.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Pike is the only person known to have survived an execution attempt after getting a lethal injection in the United States.

Pike, along with her then-boyfriend and another young woman, tortured and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, in 1995. Pike, who was 18, is the only one of the three with a death sentence. The boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, was ineligible for the death penalty because he was 17. The other woman, Shadolla Peterson, testified against Pike and Shipp and was given probation.

articles.title: 2 dead, 860K without power from Hurricane Isaias

paras.en: Oct. 9 (UPI) -- Hurricane Isaias landed near Destin, Fla., Friday evening, and was downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone, bringing high winds, rain and flooding.
One person in Escambia County, Fla., died "due to a downed tree," county officials said, and another was killed in Birmingham, Ala. Both were killed when trees fell on homes.
Across the southeastern United States, about 860,000 people were without power Saturday, with trees and power lines down.
Emergency management in Santa Rosa County, Fla., situated between Pensacola and Destin, said the majority of roads in the county are "impassable due to down trees and/or power lines."
More than 80% of customers were without power, and wind gusts rose to more than 100 mph Friday night.
Thirty teams from the Florida Department of Transportation are assessing damage Saturday in the Panhandle.

"At first light, thousands of linemen and utility crews have convoyed from Sandestin and along the I-10 corridor to get to work, focusing on outages in the hardest hit communities," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said.
"It was pitch black out. The storm had passed. It was safe enough to go out, and they were doing it," he added.
Some airports in the area have reopened. Northwest Florida Beaches Airport reopened to commercial service, but the Destin, Fort Walton Beach and Pensacola airports are still closed.

Heavy rainfall will move quickly into the Tennessee Valley and southern Appalachians. Flash flooding and landslides are possible, especially in mountainous areas, the National Hurricane Center said in its 4 a.m. CDT Saturday update.
Isaias was about 105 miles south of Birmingham, Ala., and about 25 miles south-southeast of Mobile, with maximum sustained winds of about 35 mph. There are no more weather warnings in effect.
Isaias is the first hurricane of the year in the Atlantic basin, despite a strong El Niño.
Through the weekend, Isaias is expected to bring 4 to 8 inches of rainfall across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle, the Big Bend region and southwest Georgia.
Localized totals up to 15 inches were also possible across the Panhandle and Big Bend.
Forecasters expected the coastal Carolinas to receive 2 to 5 inches of rain, with localized totals up to 10 inches also possible.
The remainder of the Southeast was forecast to get 2 to 5 inches. A risk for tornadoes will persist through Saturday afternoon across parts of the eastern Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.
Wind shear in the Atlantic has kept hurricanes at bay so far this season, but low wind shear in the Gulf helped Isaias.

articles.title: For World Mental Health Day, a check-up on the music industry
articles.author: Walaa Elsiddig

paras.en: When Olivia Rodrigo dropped her third studio album You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, it quickly became one of the year’s biggest breakouts, with legions of fans seeing themselves in its melancholy themes of sadness, loneliness and heartache. On the standout track “what’s wrong with me,” she opens the song with a wrenching and telling line: “I’m just staring at the ceiling, can’t describe this feeling.” Luckily, she was fibbing on that last part: Rodrigo has a knack for describing the depths of despair, and making us all feel a little less alone as a result – with Grammy nominations possibly waiting in the wings as a result.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Rodrigo’s album would make the perfect soundtrack for today’s World Mental Health Day. An annual tradition since 1992, it’s a moment to acknowledge that, like Rodrigo bravely points out, we’re not alone in our struggles. In Billboard’s latest episode of their Like Minded series in partnership with BetterHelp, Monaleo and Kehlani discussed motherhood and the permission to take care of oneself. “63% of U.S. women struggle to prioritize their health,” as reported in the launch of The Permission Project, a BetterHelp initiative focused on women’s mental health.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Between giving yourself permission and this year’s theme of World Mental Health Day, Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change, it all coincides with the music industry’s intimate relationship with mental health and giving oneself the OK to seek help. In the past year, the music world saw a genre-spanning slate of artists both wearing their hearts on their sleeves in their art, as well as publicly prioritizing their own mental health like never before.

Proving that it doesn’t matter whether you’re a fledgling singer-songwriter playing coffee shops and looking for a break, or the record-breaking artist Ella Langley, struggles don’t discriminate. Langley, who is breaking Billboard Hot 100 records as of late with her No. 1 smash “Choosin’ Texas,” has regularly sung about mental health and feeling less than. Take, for instance, “Be Her,” Langley’s vulnerable single from sophomore album Dandelion. On the song, Langley talks about wanting to emulate a fellow gal she’s idolizing. “I just want to be her so bad it hurts,” she croons with a signature twang, alluding to fretting about being less-than and an empty feeling of longing.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But beyond the lyrics, Langley has prioritized her mental health even as her immense success was unfolding before her. In fact, just before the dawn of her record-breaking run, Langley canceled a chunk of her 2025 tour, writing on Instagram: “I want to be fully present for the moments ahead, and I know I can’t do that without taking care of myself,” adding, “Sometimes we have to listen when our bodies and hearts tell us to slow down.” It was a vulnerable choice, and one that eventually paid off for the current superstar: She slowed down in preparation for something better.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Prioritizing oneself is something Ariana Grande has been brave about as well, with Grande perhaps the poster child for the biggest mental health story of the year. While belting out raw anthems on her 2026 album Petal (including the emotive anti-romance ballad “Hate That I Made You Love Me”) in the wake of her stunning success with Wicked, Grande announced a hiatus from public life and canceled all engagements after her current tour, including a turn in a much-ballyhooed upcoming production of Sunday in the Park With George. Grande cited “ongoing public scrutiny,” as fans around the world then rallied to her defense about knowing when to step back from the inferno of fame. In June, Grande also launched B-Line through her Brighter Days Ahead Foundation, in support of the below-the-line workers that make the industry sing.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Langley and Grande aren’t the only ones who knew when to rest in face of a grueling schedule, which serves as popularity’s double-edged sword. Look no further than the typical vulnerability singer Lola Young exhibits, with the talented UK singer-songwriter also taking a step back from her burgeoning spotlight, which included a best new artist Grammy nomination (and best pop solo performance win for “Messy”) to work on herself amid rising fame. “It’s an ongoing process,” she said earlier this year. “I’m not the finished article, but I’m doing a hell of a lot better.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Another one of music’s biggest acts, the beloved country star Jelly Roll, has also been frank about taking care of his mental health, amid personal struggles including his recent divorce as well as being a recovering addict. “I just gotta go do a little bit of work on myself to make sure that I’m all the way ready,” he said when it comes to handling the next steps of his skyrocketing career. “I’m completely sober, though. I’m clear-headed, and I’m deep in therapy, I’m deep in my Bible, but I think that I gotta separate from the chaos of the business for me to really hear what God wants for me to do next.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: From breakouts to veteran acts, the pop songstress Meghan Trainor was so overwhelmed on the eve of her 2026 tour she pulled the plug on it entirely. Speaking to Billboard earlier this year in a candid interview, she spoke about being a brand-new mother and explained she needed help to see the bigger picture in her life amid the pressure of an impending tour. “I was drowning. I couldn’t do it all and I thought I was doing it all,” Trainor noted.

As the music industry has proven, mental health checkups are an essential part of life, including for artists who are seemingly on top of the world. It’s a worthy reminder on World Mental Health Day, and the rest of the year as well.

articles.title: Why Silver Lake’s Hottest New Hotel Took So Long to Open (Blame Katy Perry)
articles.author: Lexy Perez

paras.en: In a town where projected release dates are often missed, this is one for the record books. Hotel Lucile, a boutique hotel inside a renovated church in Silver Lake, had set a soft opening for late 2024, which was pushed to spring 2025 and then again to 2026. On Sept. 14, the 25-room property finally welcomed its first guests, marking the end of an epic, 15-year struggle to bring the 1931 property back to life. The church’s stained glass remains, as does a towering cross atop the building. The nave, meanwhile, has been reborn as a New American French restaurant, Sous Sous, with floor-to-vaulted-ceiling curtains and a hulking, marble bar.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It’s a welcome addition to a hip neighborhood long in need of a designer hotel, and location scouts for Netflix’s Nobody Wants This and HBO’s I Love LA — which both regularly shoot nearby — are likely lining up to be first inside. (The hotel’s GM, Anthony Gutierrez, won’t name names but says they’ve had multiple inquiries.) Still, anyone who lives nearby and has watched the project unfold has the same question: What took so long?

The hotel’s journey from crumbling Presbyterian church to Silver Lake hotspot is more interesting, a soap opera that involves government red tape, some nuns and Katy Perry. Of the long road, Jennifer Armbruster, president of the hotel group Casetta, the project’s developer, explains with a laugh: “The deal structure of the church, combined with COVID, combined with some permitting issues, a new city council — just all of that.”

Hotel Lucile’s origin story begins in 2011, when celebrated restaurateur Dana Hollister announced plans to turn the former Pilgrim Church into a boutique hotel. It was a good idea, but well ahead of its time. (Seco, a natural wine bar whose fans include Kaia Gerber and Olivia Rodrigo, wouldn’t open across the street for another 14 years, shortly after Erewhon moved in down the block.) And Hollister reportedly spent years fighting the city for permits to sell alcohol and allow dancing.

At the same time, Hollister was also engaged in a lengthy courtroom battle with Perry and the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Los Angeles over the rights to another property, a Los Feliz convent the singer hoped to turn into a private home. Hollister lost that fight in 2017 and sold her stake in the hotel project to cover millions in damages. In 2018, Casetta stepped in, taking over the church’s lease for what one broker estimates might have been north of $4.5 million. Right partner, poor timing. By the time the architectural plans were finished, COVID hit, and Hotel Lucile was further delayed.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The church — on the corner of Lucile Avenue and Griffith Park Boulevard — has a rich Hollywood history, having once served as the home to the groundbreaking Asian American theater company the East West Players. What made the building worth saving was also what made the project so challenging. Rehabbing historic church pillars and archways — the grand entrance that’s been an anchor of the corner — required a specialized restoration expert. After years of neglect, the once-rotating, 12-foot cross was barely attached and was nearly removed following heavy rains earlier this year.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The setbacks were costly. But the finished product is impressive. A sense of drama abounds at the hotel, which was designed by Venice-based studio Electric Bowery. The church’s center has been reborn as a 96-seat restaurant with lush velvet booths, the seasonal menu courtesy of De La Nonna chef Patrick Costa. (Local artist Janel Foo designed custom stained glass coasters inspired by the sanctuary.) The former choir loft serves as a private bar with a martini cart, while the church’s onetime playground is now home to a plunge pool and patio. In a nod to the building’s religious origins, the do-not-disturb signs read “Solitude.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Creating a sense of place was paramount and befits a property that aims to once again be part of Silver Lake’s fabric. Gutierrez likens the vibe to “your eclectic neighbor that has all this fabulous art up in almost contradictory ways but coming together in a really well-designed space,” he says, which makes sense. “We want to be good neighbors.” Amen.

articles.title: Nicolas Cage Teases ‘True Detective’ Role, Says He “Probably” Won’t Work With Prime Video Again After Refusing to Sign AI Waiver for ‘Spider-Noir’
articles.author: Lexi Carson

paras.en: Nicolas Cage says he wants to work with more Gen Z directors as Hollywood studios push more into AI.

Cage swung by New York Comic Con on Saturday morning, amid work on the film Perish in Minneapolis, as part of a “Spotlight” panel that spanned a career of critically acclaimed roles, action blockbusters, and indie and cult classics.

While discussing the future of his career and how he’s trying to survive as a film performer and actor “in a very different world that is growing exponentially with so much information so quickly,” the actor addressed his time working on the only season of Prime Video’s Spider-Noir.

“The way it’s being deployed with the gifs, and we talked about Kane Parsons and what he managed to do with ‘Still Life’ in our other conversation, it seems to me that if I could like a Cindy Sherman photograph — get the character, psych up, and then take the picture, that would communicate with the meme world we’re living in today,” he said. “[But] how can you become relevant as things are moving so fast? I’m still looking for that, and I don’t really have an exact answer for you. And I’m still trying to find it.”

paras.en: He continued: “How do you survive AI? Amazon is a very AI friendly company to the tune of 50 billion dollars invested to OpenAI. I am not an AI friendly actor. I didn’t sign the waiver to let them use AI on Spider-Noir. It’s kind of like I’m probably not going to be working with that studio again. But that’s OK. So I got to get with these young directors who are Gen Z and they’re going at it their own way, whether it’s through the YouTube culture or whatever it is. They’re doing it from scratch and by hand. I want to get with that.”

paras.en: Cage also talked about whether he’s venturing into his own YouTube or podcast work, which led him to discuss the ongoing conversation about a potential role in True Detective season five.

Right after, Cage also cracked a joke about what next movie he would get behind, and that, he said, was a National Treasure film where “Ben Gates is going after the Epstein files. That would be relevant. I’ll make that movie.”

At another point, while talking about the very-onlineness of today’s filmmaking, he shared that the pop culture meme featuring him that he doesn’t get is from The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent. “I just don’t get the Pedro Pascal, Nic Cage LSD trip. I’m like, OK, he’s got a stupid smile, and I’ve got a stupid smile. What’s the big deal?”

The rest of the conversation covered everything from Con Air and Ghost Rider to Leaving Las Vegas and Valley Girl, with Cage talking about upcoming projects as much as past ones. That includes Perish, a role he described as a trippy dream that helped him unlock the character, in which he shared he’s “wearing a rainbow artificial fur code.”

“In the dream, I was myself, and there was this little baby, and also on the other side were these beautiful ladies. They were this sort of call of the wild. ‘Nicolas, come to us, come to us.’ And I said, ‘I don’t know who this baby belongs to. I’ve got to protect the baby.’ ‘No, Nicolas, come with us, come with us. I chose the baby, even though it wasn’t my baby. I said I can’t leave a baby alone, and I woke up and I went, I just unlocked how to play the character.’”

While working with directors, Cage noted that he isn’t fond of directors who give line readings. If the director is making too many for you, “Well, why did you hire me?” A recent time the vision of a director and the actor clashed was on an upcoming project. “A movie which hasn’t come out yet called The Prince, I had these very bizarre hand gestures and the director’s [like], I’m not too sure about that. I said, ‘I really believe this is going to work… I think this is going to work,” he said. “When you see the movie, you will see that it does work.”

Or adventure films, I wanted to learn something there to see if I could do it, or do some comedy, and even within that, the different genres. I wanted to explore different styles.”
